utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and listening to us. First of all, I would like to inquire if the situation with the documents tendered by the Prosecution with Witness Dr. Hagland is solved. There are three categories of documents. The first group are those which have a translation; the second group are those the parties agree that there's no translation necessary; and the third group are those we are waiting still for the translation. Is it possible to get an update so that we have it clear on the record. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon to Your Honours; good afternoon to the Defence and everyone. I believe we can provide the Trial Chamber with some information. There -- with respect to the category 2 exhibits on which the parties -- oh, let me just -- let me start over again. With respect to the category 3 exhibits, awaiting translation, the parties are waiting translations on the following exhibits which the Defence has identified a desire for translation. So the following exhibits the Defence has told us they want translations of: That is, P01307, 1308, 1309, 1311, and 1360. Our understanding is, with respect to any other exhibits in connection with Dr. Hagland for which there is not currently a translation, the Defence has no objection to those being admitted without a translation. So it's simply the five exhibits I just enumerated which the Defence has brought to our attention and for which we are awaiting translation currently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. They are marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, we need a clarification in relation to P1360. Was that correct, that you said P1360?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. P01360.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was a document we didn't receive into evidence. It was marked but not admitted. That was, in our understanding, no translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. And my understanding is that is a document which the Defence is requesting a translation of in order for it to be admitted. That they -- they are insisting on a translation for that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will check that with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's our understanding, is we're awaiting a translation of that. And it was MFI'd for that reason. Hold on, I'm about to speak with the oracle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told by the Registry, on page 9119, lines 21 to 22, Mr. McCloskey indicated: We don't need that. And it was not tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We've come to the same conclusion, Mr. President. My understanding is that the Defence still wishes to have a translation of that exhibit for their purposes. So we can take it off the list I gave you, but I think pursuant to the Defence request it's still in the pipeline to be translated and present in e-court for future purposes, if any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is a different issue. And we will check the record and the numbers again and to make clear that we have all matters solved in this relation. The witness should be brought in, please. We go into closed session to enable the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, good afternoon, sir. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies today. Mr. Thayer has some more questions for you for exactly 18 minutes. Even three more minutes left for the examination-in-chief than you indicated yesterday, Mr. Thayer. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if I don't use those, do those three minutes roll over into my next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. We count them for the time you have exceeded your own estimation with other witnesses in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday about crossing the Drina using rubber tubes. Do you know whether other people who crossed the Drina River during this same time-period, do you know what other means they may have used to cross the river, other than rubber tubes like yourself? Do you know what other crafts or devices or ways they got across the river?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said in the camp that they had created a raft made of wood and then they managed to get across with that. But I saw from the cliffs the next day when I went out to look off the cliffs that there was some shelling in the canyon. Shells were falling into the lakes. And I managed to get across using the inner tubes of truck tires.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who or what was that shelling directed at, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't close enough to see. But I could see down in the Drina, I saw the shells, and I heard the echoes of shells down in the canyon. But I wasn't close enough to see where exactly the shells were landing or what exactly was going on because I was on a hill called Zvijezda. I think that's what it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And in your group, were there any soldiers, or was it all civilians? Was it mixed?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you crossed, was anyone armed?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody in my group was armed. There was seven of us. And when they brought us up to that other group of about 150 people who had already been captured, none of them were dressed in uniforms. They didn't have any weapons. They checked us, they searched the back-packs. We threw everything on the ground, on a tarpaulin, and there were no weapons there. I was able to see that because I was throwing my own things on that tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And within your group and from your experience in the two camps in Serbia, meeting others who had crossed the Drina during this time, tell us a little something about the composition of these groups that went across. Were they only military-aged men crossing; were there young boys; were there elderly men; were there any women who crossed the Drina during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one woman. I don't think there were children. There were older children, 14 years old. My nephew was among them, for example. And there were a few of those young youths. And this is difficult for me to say: There were some people who were mentally disabled. There was a boy in the camp with me who had difficulty speaking, and he had a very hard time because of it. He would always get beaten whenever he went to the toilet. He was also under-age.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to, previously, being held on the Serbian side in two camps, and those were Sljivovica and Mitrovo Polje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I spent one night in Sljivovica. Actually, two days; I'm not exactly sure. But I was called out and I was afraid because I thought that they were going to execute me. However, they singled out a group of about 450 men and they took us to Mitrovo Polje, which is in the south of Serbia. And that's where the second camp was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber the date of your final release from the camp.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd of January, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point were you reunited with your family, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was reunited with my family in 1996 after I'd spent six months in America with the assistance of UNHCR and ICRC. I spent some time with a family in the US. And as I was unable to connect with my family from America, I had to go back to Bosnia. I didn't know what the situation was like, whether the state of war was still on and so on. But then I

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As we are in open session, I think we need a redaction of the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you were reunited with your family, did your wife tell you about her experience being transported out of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we talked about how we survived that period. She told me about how they managed to reach the free territory in Zepa. She said that they were transported in trucks and buses. And that they weren't escorted either by UNHCR or by the ICRC. And that on their way there they were intercepted by the Chetniks, they were searched. Their valuables were taken, if anyone had any. They were threatened. And she said that in one place - I can't remember where exactly - she said they were stoned. She said that the locals had gathered, stopped the truck, and then they were stoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then they were offloaded in Tisca, which is some 6 kilometres from the free territory, and they had to walk. The trip there was quite chaotic. They were intercepted again. They were tired, hungry, frightened. That's what she told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we may go into private session for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could stay with the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could just stay with this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned some other locations in your testimony. You mentioned taking your family -- oops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, the map back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That was P104, page 13, if we need it back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you mentioned taking your family to a particular location where other people had brought their families before they were transported out of the enclave. Can you tell the Trial Chamber the name of that location where you said good-bye to your family?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left my wife and children in Stitkov Do. That's close to Zepa. Not in the centre because I couldn't go there. Chetniks had already entered Zepa. They were with the UNPROFOR. Just a moment, I can't see it here. Maybe if you could zoom it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If the -- if it's not --

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, on this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you look -- if you look just a little bit below where you've drawn that circle, sir, do you see the words Stitkov Do? If you just go down maybe an inch on your computer screen.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now I just want to ask you: Is the area that you just circled, around the two words Stitkov Do, where you dropped your family off, or did you drop your family off north of Stitkov Do, I guess, is what we just need to know?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right here. No, no, right at Stitkov Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please put an X next to that circle where you left your family.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] X, Stitkov Do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it clear on the record, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender this Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit P104 marked by the witness for the second time shall be assigned Exhibit P1816. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the just minute or so we have left, can you describe for the Trial Chamber as best as you can the emotions and the thoughts that you and, in particular, your wife had as you were making the decision to leave her and your family there and for you to separate from them. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what -- what were you thinking, what were your emotions at that time?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was extremely difficult for me. I left them there, and my hope was that they would survive. 90 per cent, that they would survive. I thought that the Red Cross would be with them and that the UNPROFOR would transport them. But I also had doubts. It was very, very difficult for me. I went back to Poljanice and I saw the footwear of other people there, and it was really difficult for me. I went back during the night. I was afraid of the shelling, because it's an open plain on the road towards Poljanice. I also didn't want to run into the Chetniks. So during the night, in the area of Vratar, you could see the houses burning. And when I was with my wife in Stitkov Do, I couldn't down to Zepa because I heard that the Chetniks were already in Zepa together with UNPROFOR. That's why I didn't bring my wife any further. That's where they were left, they spent the night there, and then they went down there and found a completely chaotic situation there. There were Chetniks with trucks, and they were loading them into the trucks and so on. That same evening or, rather, during that night, maybe it wouldn't be so difficult for me if I hadn't seen the houses burning up from the Pribijotci [phoen]. Also on the left side the houses were burning, towards Vrata; that's the name of the village. And then there's a hill called Stup close to Zepa on the left side. I returned, and I was in the hope that they would survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why did you not stay with -- stay with them and try to leave on the convoy, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this would be your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would be a suicide. Later on I heard that the group that was negotiating with the Chetniks, that they never reappeared. Avdo Palic, for instance, he was found recently. And I know nothing about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness --

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that's what helped me to make the decision not to go with the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just want a clarification to better understand the geography as well. In your testimony, you've said you crossed -- or I understand your testimony to mean you crossed across the Drina River to the Serbia -- to Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: And you were escaping from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. I escaped from Bosnia and Herzegovina. I hoped to go through Serbia and reach Macedonia because it was free down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, now it's the right of the accused, Mr. Tolimir, to put questions to you during his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, it's your turn now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Peace unto this house. I greet everybody present and the witness. And I wish for this testimony and these proceedings to end in accordance with God's will and not my will. I would also like to ask the witness, since we speak the same language, to make a short pause after I make my question and to wait until my question has appeared in the screen. He should answer only after that. And I'm going to follow the same procedure when he speaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So let us start with the most recent questions. Just now, line 13, Judge Nyambe, asked you whether you went to Serbia, and you said: Yes, I wanted to go to Macedonia. Could you tell me, why do you speak of Serbia in such a way in your statements? Because you were looking to be saved in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't looking to be saved in Serbia. I was escaping. My goal was to get to Macedonia and for that I had to go through Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 11, line 17, the Prosecutor asked you why didn't you want to go with your family. Just a moment, let me finish. And you said that you were afraid for your life. My question is: Were you more afraid for your life? How come you were not afraid for the lives of your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was afraid for the lives of my wife and children. But I heard that the Red Cross and the UNHCR and UNPROFOR were going to organise the transport and evacuation. So 90 per cent, or maybe even 99 per cent, I couldn't be sure. And I have to tell you, since I heard from the survivors of Srebrenica what really happened to them, I really wasn't certain about anything. And if I went there, 100 percent -- I'm sure 100 percent that I would have no chance, because have you to think about what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I hear what you say. But can you tell me: Was a single person killed among those who were transported by the VRS into the federation?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was anybody from the inhabitants of your place killed during the transport from your place to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 14 persons from my place in the camp but there are also those who disappeared, those who tried to go through the woods and they're completely lost now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. But they are the people taking part in combat activities. What I'm asking about is whether anybody was killed among those who went in an organised way to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdo Palic, the negotiator, and two or three other people who were with him were also killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm going to make pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I want you to tell me once again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask both speakers to pause between question and answer. The same is -- I wish for you, Mr. -- please pause and wait for a moment. You can see when the translation has finished. Then the record on the screen in front of you will stop. It is very difficult for the interpreters. Please, continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like the witness to answer my question directly, not by other questions or some other answers. I asked you: Was anybody killed among those who were transported from the centre of Zepa to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, those of military age were killed. We were told that elderly people, women, and children should go with the Red Cross. But you took 14 people and you kept them in the camp in Rogatica. And I'm talking here only about my place, people who I know. Many people who lost their way in the woods were lost. They are completely disappeared, which means that you were brutally killing them. They thought that they would survive if they went through the woods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt for a moment. Sir, we are here in the courtroom and we are trying to find out the truth. I'm don't -- I'm not quite sure if I understood you correctly when you said "you took them" from the column. If you are referring to the accused, then this is not an appropriate answer. We have to find out what happened and what is in relation to the accused in this trial. Please just tell us what you went through, what you observed, what your experiences were. And then we will find out what really happened on the ground. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like the witness, once again, to answer. Was anybody killed among the civilians, men, women, children, who were transported together with his wife from his place towards the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did your wife tell you was anybody killed in her bus?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In her bus, nobody was killed. But a number of people were killed or ended up in the camps. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You can freely tell to the Trial Chamber first and last names of all the people who were killed after the VRS took over the place and after VRS guaranteed that they would be safe during the transport.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their names. My wife didn't tell me that anybody was killed in her truck. I'm simply talking about the general situation in Zepa. There was killing. There was violence. There was torture. Many people who remained there after the fall of Zepa -- you know, UNPROFOR had absolutely no role to play. The Chetniks wouldn't allow it. It means that many people remained in the woods and they were killed off there like wild beasts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell this Trial Chamber the name of any person who remained in Zepa and who was killed and who is registered as having been killed by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hazim Sulejmanovic and his son. Hazim Sulejmanovic and his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us where they were killed and how they were killed?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are here no more. They remained in Luke. I don't know where they were killed or how they were killed, but they were killed. And it's only two people that I'm mentioning now. There are more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know anything about their killing, since you're claiming here that they were killed? You only know that they are no more. Do you know anything more?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somewhere along the way to the free territory you intercepted them -- I mean, the Chetniks intercepted them, and they did what they did during the whole war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Page 7, line 7, you said there that your family arrived in buses when you brought them to the place where you brought them - let's not mention the name - and you said that along the way the Chetniks threatened them because in the bus there wasn't anybody from ICRC or UNHCR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So if that's correct, could you tell us, please, does that mean that the Chetniks used to intercept and kill people if at the same time you say that they themselves actually transported your family?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chetniks intercepted them at a certain place. My wife doesn't know the name of that place. And all the other inhabitants gathered there and started throwing stones at them and swearing their Turkish and Balija mothers. That's 100 per cent truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you seen that yourself or have you heard it from your wife?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife told me and my children told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Uh-huh. So it's hearsay. Can you tell this Trial Chamber would it be possible for Serbs to move in such free fashion along the territory of the federation in that time during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Serbs who lived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You mean the Serbs who were in the army or those Serbs whom Izetbegovic wanted to come from Republika Srpska and live there?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Serbs normally lived in Sarajevo during the war. They were real Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you're talking about real Serbs. But can you tell us what happened to the Serbs in Smolovici? It was a small enclave in Eastern Bosnia just like Zepa.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you are asking me about something that I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But everybody in Bosnia knows about it. You know about it.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to the Serbs who lived in Smoloca [phoen] surrounded by Muslim population? Did they manage to survive until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was then in Serbia, in your General Staff. I was interrogated there right at that time, so I have no idea what was going on there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir and witness, please slow down. It's very complicated to follow this speed. And don't overlap again. Please be very careful. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I am asking you about the events in Smoloca in 1993. That's the time when you were a soldier in Srebrenica. Or maybe in 1992. So can you tell me, do you know what happened to that population? Because it was publicly announced.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about it. I have no information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's the third time, on my counting, that the accused has asked the same question of this witness and obviously the witness has given the same answer, that he doesn't know anything about it. He's mentioned the same village three times. This is wasting time and it's abusing the witness, to continue asking the same questions in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I observed earlier that you qualified an answer of the witness as hearsay. You must know you are asking for hearsay. Many questions are related to events he was not taking part in. So you should choose what you can gain from this witness as facts. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm also grateful to the Prosecutor. I'm going to try to be as efficient as he is, but I have to apologise, simply had to ask that, because this witness was avoiding to answer my question about Smoloca, saying that he was in Serbia at that time. Page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that your wife and your family were offloaded 6 kilometres from Luka. My question is: Was your family, as everybody else, offloaded in the territory which was in between the two territories, or did they offload them there on purpose, deliberately?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're misinterpreting something here. I said that my family was transported from Zepa towards the free territory. However, they were offloaded 6 kilometres from the free territory. The place is called Tisca. That was allegedly somewhere in between the borders. But it was quite far away from the borders. So she had to cover 6 kilometres on foot with the children. So I can tell you very precisely it was 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether all the inhabitants of your place were offloaded at the same spot during the transport towards the federation? And do you know that it was the army, the BiH army, who determined that spot?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I -- I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5, line 23, you said there were some under-age boys and also some mentally retarded children in the camp in Serbia where you were towards the end. So my question is as follows: Did the Serbs from Serbia invite you to come to those camps in Serbia, regardless of whether you were under-age, retarded, or elderly, or whatever? Did they invite you, or did you swim over Drina on your own?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to save myself, regardless of whether it was Serbia or wherever. My goal was Macedonia. I was afraid in Serbia as much as I was in Republika Srpska, because the Yugoslav Army also controlled everything and they did whatever they wanted, both in Serbia and in the Serbian republic. So my goal was to reach Macedonia where I could be free. And only there my life would not be in danger. My goal was not to be discovered in Serbia. But when I arrived to Serbia, I was captured, I was tortured, I ended up in the camp. I survived, barely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber why do you call Serbs the Chetniks, both in Serbia and in Republika Srpska? And in Serbia they didn't wage any war against you. And why do you call the Army of Republika Srpska a fascist army? You said that you were in Pecina - it's page 87, line 8, of yesterday's transcript - and you said that your father in the previous war was also there.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Also in the previous war my father had to flee from the Chetniks and he was hiding in that place and my mother was wounded by the Chetniks. And also, one more thing: I'm calling them Chetniks because they cannot be normal people. How can they kill a child, an elderly person, a disabled person, a huge number of people? I think they are monsters. They cannot be normal people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, did you see any of those executions with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Execution? Of course. I am from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who it was who was executed in Srebrenica by the VRS? Do you know who and when?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shells that used to land on the playground, I used to pick up those people and take them to hospital. You killed 100 people in one day and wounded 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... you -- it's not your role as a witness to say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I get carried away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I can understand that this is a very emotional situation for you, but it is not your duty to judge what this accused did or not. The question put to you was -- and it is very difficult for you to answer these questions because there's so many questions in one. One question was: Did you see any of those executions with your own eyes? With your own eyes. Could you answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. In 1993, when I was in Srebrenica, I saw that 100 people were killed in the playground and 70 wounded. I'm not talking about the playground itself, but I can say that in total 100 people were killed by the shelling at that time. And I used to collect them and take them to the hospital, both the wounded and the dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We heard about that yesterday. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that in 1993 you saw some killed and wounded people on the playground. Can you tell us, was it all captured by the camera which came with General Morillon, and was it broadcast to the world public?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that there was one man who was robbed by you. You took all his materials and all his notes. It was a German person engaged in humanitarian work in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to stop you here on two reasons. You again said: "You took all his materials and all his notes." If you -- if you are telling us that Mr. Tolimir did something, then tell us. But it's not your duty to judge what your opinion is. If you say "you," be very careful with that, please. It is the Chamber who will make a judgement at the end of this trial. And another thing. I would like to remind you to pause and not immediately to start with your answer when you get a question by Mr. Tolimir. The court recorder and the interpreters can't follow this conversation. Please bear that in mind. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. I will do my best not to do that again. I didn't mean him directly. When I said "you," I meant the army, the Serbian army. I didn't mean the accused himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation. This is much more helpful. If you can give us clear answers about the facts. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether in 1991 in Srebrenica any of the inhabitants of Srebrenica had a camera and did they film those events and was this incident that you are talking about documented?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait with your answer. Now you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met a man. He was a German who was helping to get the water works running again. He was helping the people. He had a lot of information, and he had the camera equipment. And in 1993 I heard that all of that material was confiscated from him in Zvornik. He had a camera, and he maintained some kind of record. He was a humanitarian worker. He was helping to get the water up and running again, water for washing. He was helping the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that in your previous answer. Can you just now tell us who you heard it from? And can you tell us again whether there was anybody in Srebrenica who had a camera, and was this material something that was ever brought to light? Was it broadcast by any international media? Were these cassettes preserved?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This was the only camera that I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it might be helpful to clarify the questions, which might also help clarify the answers to the Court's desire, that General Tolimir put his case directly to the witness about this issue. That is, if it is General Tolimir's case that the playground shelling that this witness testified about did not happen, if it is General Tolimir's case that witness is making that up, and I gather that that is somewhat his case, given the questions about whether it was captured on camera, then he should just put that directly to the witness. He has an obligation to put his case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see any problem with the question if there was anybody in Srebrenica who had a camera. This was the question. And the witness answered: I don't know. I think this is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm not objecting to the question, Mr. President. I'm just trying to suggest, under the Rules, that the General put his case to the witness. And if it is his case, again, that this playground massacre that we heard about didn't happen, that it's propaganda or a mere allegation or whatever, that he put that to this witness directly and not beat around the bush.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have something else. My brother was killed in 1994 by a shell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... please wait. We are conferring at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, the Chamber is of the view that it is the right of the accused to put questions during the cross-examination to the witness without putting his theory about the events and his estimation of the events happening in Srebrenica at the relevant time to the witness first. We wouldn't agree with such a rule. Mr. Tolimir is not giving evidence. He may put questions to the witness to find out what he knows about these events. That's all during cross-examination. And that has to do with finding out the truth and testing the credibility of a witness. This is all in our view. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on with your questions. Let me remind you not to put too many questions in one. This is very difficult for the witness. And ask for facts. This is much more helpful for your case. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Three questions ago I asked you, yesterday, on page 9872, lines 3 to 6, when you were describing the place where you were hiding in July 1995, you said the following. I quote: "During World War II, my father used the same cave to hide from the Chetniks and the fascists." Later, in other line, you said that the name of the cave was Sokolina. Now, are you aware or do you know on whose side did the Muslims in Zepa fight in the course of World War II?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I say that they were partisans as well. I don't know if there were any -- I don't know which army my father was in. I don't know. But there were partisans as well, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me why in your statement you call Chetniks -- well, you called the Serbs Chetniks and fascists. Is this a pejorative name or is this an official name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... Mr. Tolimir, this is the second time you put this question to the witness and you received already an answer to that. You received an answer. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But he didn't tell me last time either why he called Serbs Chetniks and fascists. He didn't answer me, so that's why I asked him again.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all Serbs. I don't call all Serbs fascists and Chetniks. Those who killed and who expelled the Muslim people. Well, actually, not just the Muslims; they expelled and killed others. Croats, the Roma, Jews. How many Croats did you leave behind in Srebrenica or Roma? How many Roma are there left there Srebrenica? After you expelled the Muslims, did you leave Croats and Roma behind? Are there any left in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to answer my question, please. You didn't answer my question earlier. Why do you call Serbs Chetniks and fascists?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't call all Serbs Chetniks and fascists, only those monsters, those people who kill children, who kill elderly people. I don't know what to say. People who were not normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This examination is getting very complicated. First of all, I have to remind the witness, again, that it is not acceptable if you say: After you expelled the Croats. This is the Chamber to decide on that. Secondly, please calm down. And I know that very well, that you are in a very difficult situation and that you are very emotional. It was a clear question of Mr. Tolimir, although it was the third time he put it to you. Mr. Thayer, you are right. I think that what you wanted to raise for the third time. But every time in a slightly different way. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just -- Mr. President, and that might also, perhaps to some small degree, help the temperature a little bit to stop asking the same question over and other again. That can only help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We received an answer to that question by the witness. It is his point of view. And we all are in the position to judge why that happened. Please carry on. And not the same question again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court now show document 1D587, page 2, paragraph 1, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now look at page 2, after we look at page 1. We can see the signature. We can see that the witness signed this signature -- signed this statement. Thank you. Can we now look at page 2, paragraph 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You gave the statement in March 1992. Sorry. In 2002 -- March 2002, I apologise. And you said in the statement that the fact that you did not enjoy freedom of movement means that you cannot return back to the place where you lived. You said that. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember everything that I said in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you answer my question then? Did anyone forbid you from entering the territory of Republika Srpska where your place of birth is?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Republika Srpska didn't exist at the time. It was Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then there was the Yugoslav Army who captured that area and who expelled the people, persecuted the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was talking about 2002, when you gave your statement. You said: The fact that I do not have the freedom of movement means that I cannot go back to the place where I lived.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Only in 2005 was I able to go. And I was very much afraid. Even now when I go, I'm still afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm sorry because I need to put this question to you again. My question is: Did anybody forbid you, in 2002, from entering the area of Republika Srpska and going back to your place?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2002 it was still unsafe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I will always interrupt you if you are overlapping in this way. It is impossible to continue in that way. Please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't do it again, Your Honours. I apologise. I really do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, if somebody was restricting your freedom of movement in 2002 in Republika Srpska, can you please tell us who that was? You said that it wasn't safe.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to tell you if you tell me the number of people who were back there, who had returned to live there in 2002, then I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, this is not an appropriate answer. You were asked by Mr. Tolimir -- no, don't interrupt me. You were asked if anybody was restricting your freedom of movement in 2002 in the Republika Srpska. Please answer the question, if you know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know. Nobody was forbidding it, but it was unsafe. It was risky, in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the first page again of this statement, 1D587. We don't need to broadcast it publicly. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see the date here of the interview. This is the third line from the bottom. It says 11th of March, 2002; 12th of March, 2002; and 13th of March, 2002. My question is: These dates in March 2002, do they correspond to the days that you were interviewed by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The dates do match. I was talking to the lawyer. Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at 1D582 now, please. 1D582.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This should not be broadcast --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doesn't need to be broadcast. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question -- well, I can see Mr. Thayer is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... before you put this question to -- before you put the question to the witness, we must make a redaction of the transcript where the place of residence is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, in addition, there's a redaction at page 32, line 9, a specific reference to a name that needs to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Indeed, that will be redacted as well. Mr. Tolimir, put your question to the witness as indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please. You wanted to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this. At the beginning of your statement you said that you had no freedom of movement. And at the very end of your statement, on page 13 in the Serbian and page 12 in the English, you said that you had come to Sweden illegally, in the country where you were, and that you sought asylum there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... now we are -- we have to go into private session. If you are dealing with this problem extensively, we can't do it in open session. First we go into private session. We have to redact the last question again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, we must have our first break now for half an hour, and we will resume at quarter past 4.00. The Court Usher will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination. And, again, I would like to remind both speakers not to be too emotional, not to overlap, to speak slowly. And if there are reasons to go into private session, Mr. Tolimir, you should consider that. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, at the end of the previous session, we were talking about the demining agency. And my question is this: Since there were many unemployed in Bosnia, and you had come from abroad, you decided to apply in the agency for demining?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got a direct job because there was a job advertisement, and I applied. This was an agency that worked in cooperation with the army and with the UN.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter didn't catch the last end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Chamber what the MPRI was? Because you worked there.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an international organisation for demining. It's BH MAK. I believe that you also know about it because the Serbian army is also engaged in demining.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell us if it's a non-governmental organisation or if it's an organisation of the Government of B&H or the Army of B&H? Who finances it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question wasn't precise. Are you talking about the BH MAK or the MPRI?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who's financing the MP -- the BH MAK and who's financing the MPRI?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mister, could you please repeat your answer. You were starting too early again. The interpreters didn't hear you. What was your answer? You were asked: Who is financing the BH MAK and the MPRI, I think it should read. Who is financing that? Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The BH MAK is being financed by the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's an organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina for demining, the demining of the field. And the MPRI is an international organisation for the clearing and removal of mines from the field. The MPRI is probably financed by the UN. It's a legal organisation. And the BH MAK is a state organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gajic, I saw you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there were some problems with the interpretation. We didn't have it for a long time. That's why I was on my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you serve in the engineers in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I swore my oath to the JNA. I served in Nis. And I was in an engineers company. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, 1D587 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have it up on the screen. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that in late June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- you left your father's village and went through the woods towards Srebrenica. My question is this: In that period, in June of 1992 that you talk about, was Srebrenica under the control of the BH Army, and was the whole road from your father's village under the control of the BH army, and had all Serbs been expelled from Srebrenica or killed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the road from my father's village towards Srebrenica, I passed through the woods. And at the time, Muslims were living in Srebrenica. I don't know about Serbs. I didn't see anyone. Could you please be more specific with your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Serbs live in Srebrenica before the war? And what happened to them in the period when you came to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, there were as many Serbs, almost as many Serbs, in Srebrenica as Muslims. And when the war began -- when the war began, they probably left. I don't know. When I arrived Srebrenica, there were no Serbs there. Actually, there was. There was an old woman who lived in my neighbourhood. Her name was Mira. And she left with some refugees in Potocari. She left on the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, on page 9840, you were asked by the Prosecutor: Were you a member of the BiH army while you were in Srebrenica? To which you answered: I don't know that there was an army there. How can you define an army? But there were some organised village guards. My question is: Since we are talking here about 1992 and 1993, did the BiH army, at the time, was it present in Srebrenica? And did it undertake offensive activities towards the territories inhabited by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the most important thing was to save what could be saved. I arrived to Srebrenica and I immediately went to be a part of the village guards. At that time, there was no organised army. And those people who managed to survive in Bratunac did the same thing. They went to the border in order to save their families and themselves, to defend themselves from the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to say whether in 1992 and 1993 there was a BiH army in Srebrenica or not.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, probably they made some lists. An army did not exist. You know what is an army. An army has the soldiers, the equipment, the weapons, everything. You can't call this an army, during 1992 and 1993, while it was a demilitarised zone, all the way up to 1995, until the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have in e-court D120. Thank you. I think the Prosecutor doesn't want it to be broadcast outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please take a look at the paragraph 3. That would be the fifth line from the top. "On the 1st of January, 1994, in Srebrenica, Strictly Confidential Order 14/75-156/93, issued by the armed forces Supreme Command staff, the unit has been in existence since 20th of May, 1992, under the name Srebrenica TO staff, or the Srebrenica armed forces staff, which was legalised by the decision issued by the staff of the BH armed forces Supreme Command, Strictly Confidential 14/76-8, dated 3rd of October, 1993."

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this is 1994. I wasn't in Srebrenica in 1994. It is possible that later on when there was peace in the demilitarised zone that they were drawing up some lists and organised some armies. But this was an army without weapons because it was a demilitarised zone in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I don't know you said the Prosecution doesn't want to have this broadcast. I don't see any reason for that. Or that's a misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I was told it's a confidential exhibit in evidence. Indeed, it should not be broadcast. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness to take a look at the third line, actually, sixth of seventh line, where it says: "The unit has been in existence since the 20th of May, 1992, under the name Srebrenica TO staff." My question is: Was there a unit in existence in Srebrenica since the 20th of May, 1992, just as it is described here? And was it legalised by the Main Staff of the Bosnian army in 1993?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are probably talking about the lists of the guards, of the TO. I was there, and I certainly would have went into their -- I certainly would have worked with them had I known that they were there. They were self-organised guards. People were afraid. People in Bratunac went and assembled in the playground of their own free will. All places that were free had to somehow defend themselves. And I also thought it's better if I start the defence here instead of waiting for them to come to my house and slaughter my children. As for the lists, I wouldn't know about that. I wasn't in the military. I can't explain you about these things. In 1992, I was a member of the village guard. I was wounded there. And then I did not perform the guard duty until the fall of Zepa, in 1995. Until just before the fall of Zepa. Then I did a few shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at paragraph with number 3 in this document. You see number 3? And just below, take a look at the following paragraph: "From 20th of April, 1992, to 12th of July, 1992, an area inside the Potocari region was liberated." And then the following paragraph: "In the period between the 2nd of May, 1992, until the 6th of August, 1992, the territory in Suceska region was liberated." And then the following paragraph: "Between the 7th of May and the 2nd of June, 1992, an area in the Kragljivoda region was liberated." And then the following paragraph: "Between the 7th of May, 1992, and 7th of May" [as interpreted] "1992, the region of Osmace was liberated." And then the following paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down. Please slow down. You are very fast while reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The following paragraph, the last on this page that can be seen, goes as follows: "In the period between the 16th of May, 1992, and the 30th of June, 1992, a territory within the zone of Skenderovici was liberated." And then after that: "In the period between the 8th of August, 1992, and the 20th of January, 1993, offensive combat activities were carried out in order to finally oust the occupying force from the municipalities of Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, and Zvornik." The most significant battles were carried out as follows: Enemy driven out from Jezestica on the 8th of August, 1992. Seizure of Podravanje on the 24th September, 1992. Battle for Fakovic on 5th of October, 1992. Return of Kamenica on the 6th of November, 1992; it's Christmas. Then return of territory in the Voljavica zone. And so on and so forth. So my question is: Does this document depicts the activities that were carried out from 1992 onwards related to the expulsion of Serbian population from the villages where they used to live? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about this document and I'm not the right person to talk about it. As far as the things that you mentioned, Osmace, that was a Muslim village. Suceska, it was a purely Muslim village. Luke, it was also a purely Muslim village with no Serbs. I suppose that you should have read that too. So it wasn't really a liberation. They were already there, and they organised themselves to protect themselves so that the Chetniks could not come in. As far as these other activities, I heard about them, but I did not take part in them, and I cannot talk about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is as follows. While in 1992 you took part in, as you put it, guards. Did this unit of guards in which you were took part in any of the actions I mentioned so far?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was wounded in 1992. It was in the beginning. Which month was it? I was wounded quite soon, so I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Here, in the second paragraph from the bottom, you can see: "In the period between the 16th of May, 1992, and the 30th of June, 1992," and you can see what took place. Were you during this period member of this so-called guards? This thing that you call guards?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, guards. I was in Likari. That's where I was guard and that's where I was wounded. After that, I did not take part in the guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell the Trial Chamber the names of your commanders, of your squad, of your platoon, of your company?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was chosen by us. It was Zuhrija Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that this document describes units in Srebrenica that carried out combat in the wider area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that it was later on registered as such. I'm not appraised of these things. These documents, these dates, I don't know anything about it. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the settlement mentioned in this document contained any Serbs? Because you said that they were allegedly liberated by the BiH army, so I want to know whether Podravanje, Kravica, and others had any Serbs in them? Potocari as well.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No Podravanje, Serbs used to live. In Potocari, I don't know. I don't know the national composition of the villages. I didn't go around the villages to find out who lived where. I know that there were Serbs in Podravanje, that there were Serbs in Kravica. There were some places that were of mixed ethnicity, where Muslims and Serbs lived side by side. I cannot be more precise about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise to the interpreters. How come that the Muslims went on to liberate Podravanje when there were Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part in that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were asked by the Prosecutors about the attack on the village of Kravica in January 1993. On page 9841, lines 5 to 12, you said, and I quote: "The Trial Chamber heard the testimony about the Bosniak attack on the village of Kravica on the Serbian Orthodox new year in the January 1993. Do you remember that this took place and is it true?" And here is your answer: "I know that it happened. I did not take part in this" -- excuse me, I have to finish the quote -- "I did not take part in this because I was wounded. The reason for this was the grate lack of food at the time," and so on and so forth. And then you said that they went there because of the food. My question is: Had you not been wounded, would you have taken place in this attack on Kravica?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have to because my children had nothing to eat. If I were in their place, in the place of those people, I would certainly go. They were also civilians. It was an invasion. That's how they described it. That's what they said, the people who returned from there bringing food. Everybody went there. Women, children, everybody. Because hunger was so terrible that they had nothing to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take part in any similar action before that?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that it was unarmed population who went to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I said. It was a huge mass of women, children, men. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that 38 people were killed and 30 people were wounded in this attack on Kravica? Can something like this be done by unarmed women and children?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the killed because I was not there and I was not informed about it. I think that it was an army, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So if it was an army, does that mean that there was an army in Srebrenica, or was it an unarmed population who went into attack?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that the killed were the members of an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I had -- I stopped you because you were overlapping again. We want -- and it is -- it should be your desire to have a clear record and a full record. Now put your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you tell us, those unarmed civilians, did they manage to kill those armed soldiers, the Serbs that you mentioned, among whom there were 38 killed and 30 wounded? And all this happened in Kravica on the 6th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, those people who were active, who had guns, they had to go and seek food. That's absolutely certain. And there was also a mass of civilians. So the cause of all this was the food. I regret if there were innocent victims there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When Muslims are killed, do you say -- well, you say that they were killed by Chetniks. When Serbs are killed, you said it was the civilians trying to grab food and that Serbs were killed in some armed actions organised by the Muslims? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're trying to say with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you said five questions ago that there were no soldiers in Srebrenica in 1992 and 1993, the period that we're talking about, perhaps later there was some record of that there were village guards. I'm asking you now, did the Serbs kill themselves? Why don't we also say that the Serbs got killed just like the Muslims got killed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your question. I would like you to be a bit more specific so that I can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple of observations, Mr. President. I'm not objecting to the line of questioning, although I think the utility is extremely limited at this point, given the many questions on this issue. I just want to note for the record: I don't believe it fairly or accurately characterises the witness's prior testimony and his answers that there were no soldiers in the enclave. I think he's been very clear that there were armed village guards. He quibbled about whether you could call it an army. But it might also help to just keep the answers clearer if the questions are a little more accurate. That's why I'm standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my observation as well. The witness -- Mr. Tolimir, that was my observation as well. The witness was denying that there was an army in the enclave. I didn't -- I don't recall that he said there was no soldier. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Could the e-court now please show D160. This is Bozo Momcilovic's statement, who testified yesterday and to whose testimony the Prosecutor referred during the questioning of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I provided the reference about what the Prosecutor asked you. Now I'm going to quote what the witness who testified yesterday, before you, said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2, please, of the statement. D160, please. D160. This is not what I'm asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we just need to get this off the screen immediately, Mr. President, because it's sensitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. We should remove it immediately, please. Thank you. D160. It was D160. Please, Mr. Tolimir, check the number of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is document D160, and this is public document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we just had just the wrong document on the screen. Wait a moment. We'll find out if we get the right one now. I think now we have the statement of Bozo Momcilovic. This was the witness of yesterday. And this is not under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we look at page 2, please. Paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we're going to look at the first paragraph. It begins from the fifth -- actually, the sixth line from the top. I'm reading from the first paragraph, line 6, on this page that I can see. Thank you. I would go -- "I frequently visited my parents and I was in Kravica on the Orthodox Christmas Day of 7 January 1993 when the Muslims attacked my village. My father didn't want to withdraw with the refugee column and abandon his home. I found him on the 17th of March of the same year, when the village was liberated. He was lying dead in front of the house and his head had been cut off and thrown next to a fence nearby. His house had been destroyed as had all the other houses in the village," and so on. From the statement -- this is from the statement of that witness. And this is what the witness replied to a question. And then after that, I will put my question to you. First I went to present to you what the witness said yesterday during the examination-in-chief in answer to a question about this matter. Thank you. On page 9807, lines 9 to 11, the question was put to the witness: Could you please say if there were any attacks on other Serbian villages in the environs of Srebrenica in 1992, 1993, and 1994, if you know? Answer by Witness Momcilovic. I quote: In 1993, when Kravica was torched ... Skelani were also torched, a village which was attacked on the 16th or 17th. Other than Bratunac, all the villages were attacked and destroyed starting from mid-May. On page 9807, lines 20 to 25, and page 9808, I ask him: Could you repeat for the transcript, please, who attacked these other Serbian villages after the 7th of January, 1993? And which villages were destroyed in 1993 by the Muslims? Thank you. And the witness replied: Under the command of Commander Naser Oric, who was headquartered in Srebrenica, the villages along the river Drina were torched; these were Fakovici, Bjelovac, Skelani. All of that happened in one day, all the small villages around Bratunac and Srebrenica and the whole of Kravica in 1993. After that, there were other villages that were destroyed from May to August. This means that up until mid-May Bratunac was the only village that had not fallen in that area where we were. Perhaps some other villages along the Drina. My question is: Was this combat carried out by Muslim civilians or by Muslim village guards, or was this done in an organised manner by the Muslim army which attacked these villages and destroyed them just like Witness Momcilovic said?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the innocent victims. I need to say that. Please believe me that those village guards at the time were village guards. Everybody knows what a soldier looks like. A soldier has a rifle, he has everything with him. You cannot have a soldier with a hunting rifle. For sure there were some victims. There must have been victims for sure. But the cause for that, the greatest cause for that, was hunger. That was something that prompted people to go back to the places where they were living. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, if you remember, as an inhabitant of Srebrenica, if, in late 1993 and early 1994, the Serbian army set off to help the Serbian population, to save it from attacks that were carried out by Muslims at Serb villages? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, I left in July to live in the place where my parents lived, so I don't know what was going on in Srebrenica. I wasn't a soldier either, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you in Srebrenica during the time Morillon was there? Because earlier you talked about some events about a playing field. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was when the shelling of the school happened and where the -- that's when Morillon was there. This involved the school playground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that March 1993?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if that was when the Serbian army carried out combat actions in relation to Srebrenica, the Muslim enclave from which attacks were carried out and from where inhabitants of Serbian villages were killed?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now, please, your answer. It was too early, your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. Perhaps I am experiencing some panic. I was interrogated in camps. So what I'm doing is not something that I'm doing deliberately. Now I can answer the question. It was noticeable. The villages that were still free, those inhabitants came to Srebrenica, which was already overpopulated, over crowded, so you could feel that. It's true that that's why the United Nations came. Philip Morillon was there because of that. The United Nations took control there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the conflict between the Muslims and the Serbs in Srebrenica ended with the proclamation of the demilitarised zone in May 1993? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know the demilitarised zone was declared. I was really happy. We were told that it was the end of the war, that there would be no more. I was overjoyed. But I still experienced worst things until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us if there were actions on both sides in Srebrenica in early 1993 and in late 1994 when you were still in Srebrenica before you went to Luke?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left to the place where my parents lived in June 1993. I don't remember the exact date, but it was definitely June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your answers to a number of my questions, you said that before the signing of the agreement there were no soldiers in Srebrenica, only the village guards and unarmed -- the unarmed population.
